records.name: Cayman Islands
records.summary:
Cayman law never held the criminalisation its earlier profile asserted: same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2001 through an Order in Council imposed from London after the local legislature refused, albeit with an unequal age of consent surviving the reform. In 2020 the Court of Appeal held that a same-sex couple's overseas marriage must be recognised, and in July 2021 roughly 600 people — including the premier, the governor and other ministers — joined the islands' first Pride parade, one of the broadest official turnouts a community there has seen.

The sharp turn came in 2022: a statute confining family status to heterosexual marriage took effect and, in March of that year, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council rejected the challenge to it. Same-sex couples therefore have no marriage or civil-partnership status, the country that administers defence and foreign affairs declined to force the issue, and equality advocates have operated mainly through immigration and recognition rulings rather than family law itself.

sources.summary: PinkNews (11 Aug 2009): UK MPs on the Foreign Affairs Committee criticised the Cayman Islands' draft constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission 'deplorable' and warning the drafting could leave Cayman courts affording citizens less protection than the European Convention on Human Rights Art 14 requires; the FCO countered that the discrimination-grounds list was open-ended. Early-dated evidence of London–local friction over LGBT protections that frames the later recognition rulings.

Cayman News Service (29 Jul 2021): around 600 people — including the premier, the governor, ministers and MLAs — joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade (Sat 7 Aug 2021 debut), an historic turnout with broad official participation; participants were asked to refrain from excessive displays of affection (organisers' condition amid public-space sensitivities). Evidence of high official tolerance in the tourist-facing environment.

Washington Blade (30 Dec 2020): immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder (wed in Ireland), the Court of Appeal holding that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds; recaps that Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie had struck down the same-sex marriage ban in March 2019 (later overturned on appeal, Aug 2019 — the recognition-for-immigration-effects line survived). Core source for the 'recognition without status' travel posture.

records.name: British Virgin Islands
records.summary:
Same-sex intimacy in the British Virgin Islands was decriminalised in January 2001 by order of the administering state's Privy Council, after the local legislature refused to act — a local legislator's 'there is nothing we can do about it' captured the resentment with which the reform landed. Family status remains contested rather than settled: in 2022 the Court of Appeal refused the local churches council's attempt to appeal a judgment in favour of two women, married in the UK, who were seeking recognition of their marriage and a declaration that the prohibition is unconstitutional — the court finding the proposed appeal had no realistic prospect of success.

Visitors encounter a tolerant-but-quiet society: travel surveys rate these twin islands among the more gay-welcoming in the Caribbean while noting resistance beneath the surface, with most local hostility 'silent and invisible' and most visitors hardly noticing either way. Discretion, not danger, is the operative norm.

sources.summary: AP report (Jan 2001) republished by GLAPN: Britain scrapped the homosexuality laws in its five remaining Caribbean territories -- including the British Virgin Islands -- by Privy Council order after local legislatures refused to act; local legislator Orlando Smith conceded 'there is nothing we can do' -- the decriminalisation moment for this territory.

GlobalGayz profile (Aug 2012/2017): the BVI is among the more gay-welcoming islands in the Caribbean but with 'silent and invisible' native homophobia and secret lives -- undated snapshot of the social climate for gay visitors.

BVI News (29 Jul 2022): the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal case-management orders (Justice Adrian Jack) in the case testing recognition of the UK same-sex marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome -- litigation over whether same-sex marriages are valid under BVI law.

records.name: Anguilla
records.summary:
Anguilla's prohibitions were removed around 2000-2001 — a recent first-person travel account puts the change at 2000, the contemporaneous wire coverage of the Caribbean-wide reform at January 2001 — again by imposition from London after local reluctance; the earlier profile's 'decriminalised 2019' appeared in no source and has been deleted. Same-sex relationships are simply not an issue in the public sense because there is almost no public LGBT life: no community organisations, no venues, no Pride, a handful of hotels marketed to gay travellers and same-sex wedding tourism pitched on 'friendly, relaxed atmosphere.'

A queer family travelling openly in 2023 described the experience as uneventful on a 35-square-mile island. The practical visitor picture is quiet neutrality — nothing protects you much, and little opposes you at all.

sources.summary: GlobalGayz country report on Anguilla (2012): profile of a 35-square-mile island about 100 miles east of the British Virgin Islands, framing gay life against dependent-territory law — Britain holds ultimate legal authority and decriminalisation came by British order rather than local repeal, with local religious protest against the change; Anguilla never had the exact prohibition law itself in the same form.

Commercial destination-wedding page for Anguilla: states plainly that 'Same-sex marriage is not currently recognized under the law in Anguilla', while marketing the island's venues for ceremonies — useful as a practical marker that only symbolic ceremonies are possible for same-sex couples there.

Associated Press via SodomyLaws (Jan 5, 2001): Britain's Privy Council ordered decriminalisation of private consensual same-sex conduct in five Caribbean territories — Anguilla, Cayman Islands, British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and Turks and Caicos — acting unilaterally after local legislatures refused to repeal, drawing protests from religious leaders.

AFAR first-person travel piece (Jun 2023): a queer family's visit finds gay sex legal in Anguilla through the British decriminalisation order (article says 2000) but a muted, not 'out and proud' scene rooted in that imposed colonial legacy rather than local choice; notes roughly 15,000 residents as one reason the gay scene stays small.

records.name: Montserrat
records.summary:
Same-sex activity is legal in Montserrat: its prohibitions were swept away in January 2001 by the same Order in Council that overrode the region's reluctant legislatures — the earlier claim of 'archaic criminal provisions on the books' was contradicted by the territory's own sources and has been removed. What public LGBT life existed was effectively extinguished twice by disaster: the 1989 hurricane and the 1995 volcanic eruptions that buried the southern half of the island and depopulated it, leaving a scatter of survivors in the north and a gay presence described as 'decimated', only partially recovered.

Local religious leaders called the 2001 reform 'totally unacceptable,' and the territory appeared resigned to following London's order. Visitors today find a tiny, dispersed, private society where neither hostility nor community is much visible.

sources.summary: GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in Montserrat' (Sept 2012): a 104 km2 island reshaped by Hurricane Hugo (1989) and the 1995 Soufriere Hills eruption that wastelanded the south and displaced over half the population north; gay life barely exists locally ('gays are everywhere but hardly here') — decimated social scene; dated but concrete.

Associated Press report (Jan 2001, via GLAPN): Britain scrapped the anti-gay statutes in five Caribbean territories including Montserrat and Turks & Caicos, saying they violated signed international human rights agreements — the legal basis on which Montserrat's prohibitions were eventually swept away; local politicians and religious leaders opposed, framed as a cultural rift with London.

records.name: Turks and Caicos Islands
records.summary:
Turks and Caicos decriminalised same-sex activity in 2001 through the UK-imposed Caribbean reform, and its constitution now bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The live frontier has been recognition rather than criminal law: the Court of Appeal ordered a residence permit for the same-sex spouse lawfully married abroad, holding that 'spouse' in the immigration ordinance must include same-sex spouses and declaring violations of the equality, non-discrimination and private-and-family-life guarantees — while declining to touch the constitution's male-female marriage definition, which it treated as controlling.

The administering state's passport guidance maintains a standing profile of the territory's rules on marriage, civil partnerships, adoption and gender recognition. Socially, a resident's account described 'virtually nothing' documented about gay life — in a territory where around two-thirds of inhabitants are themselves not native-born — so visitor experience runs on privacy and the resort economy rather than any visible scene.

sources.summary: GlobalGayz resident account ('Eddi', May 2009): documents how invisible gay life is — 'virtually nothing on the Internet about gay life in TCI'; notes ~2/3 of residents are not originally from the islands and full-citizen Belongers are a demographic minority versus foreigners, so there is no visible scene and privacy is the norm; useful as the on-the-ground social-climate read for a visitor.

UK HM Passport Office knowledge-base profile (Crown copyright 2025): official operational guidance covering nationality, legitimacy, adoption, gender recognition, civil partnerships and marriage, and documents for the territory — states adoption is legal and that 'transgender citizens are recognised in the Turks and Caicos Islands', i.e. the administering state's passport office handles gender-recognised documents for this jurisdiction.

TC Weekly News: Court of Appeal landmark ruling ordered the Director of Immigration to issue a residence permit to Timothy Haymon as the same-sex spouse of Richard Sankar — refusal on sexual-orientation grounds contravened constitutional guarantees; 'spouse' in the Immigration Ordinance read to include a same-sex spouse lawfully married in another jurisdiction, with equality/non-discrimination/private-life guarantees invoked (marriage definition left untouched). Directly relevant: same-sex partners of visitors/residents get residence recognition.

Klshepedia overview (published Apr 2026): same-sex sexual activity legal in the Turks and Caicos Islands since 2001 and discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds is constitutionally banned — the two anchor legal facts for a visitor assessing exposure.

records.name: Falkland Islands
records.summary:
South Atlantic island settlement with its own assembly: same-sex activity legal since 1989, equal age of consent since 2005, and full equality in April 2017 when the assembly approved same-sex marriage and civil partnerships 7-1, on a public consultation showing 90 per cent support for marriage and 94 per cent for partnerships — the registrar confirmed the law the following June, adoption followed the same year, the constitution bans sexual-orientation discrimination, and the first Pride was held in the capital that April. An official of the community described it as 'open, tolerant and respectful'; note that the much more remote dependencies administered from the same capital did not follow on marriage.

The earlier profile's inherited arithmetic and its borrowed UK custody stories have been deleted: on the surviving evidence the legal picture here is stronger, not weaker, than the administering state's, and there is no source indicating the GB single-sex-services code extends to the territory.

sources.summary: PinkNews (12 Apr 2017): the Legislative Assembly passed same-sex marriage (7-1) plus civil partnerships open to same-sex AND opposite-sex couples, after a public consultation showing 90% support for same-sex marriage and 94% for civil partnerships in the ~3,000-resident territory — the operative equality reform.

Rob Salerno blog (22 Jun 2017): direct confirmation from the Falklands registrar general that the March-passed same-sex marriage and civil partnership bill is law (royal-assent confusion resolved by her reply); same registrar confirms same-sex marriage is NOT legal in the South Georgia and South South Sandwich Islands dependency.

Mirror summary of the Wikipedia LGBTQ rights page (wiki-derived): legal since 1989, equal age of consent since 2005; same-sex marriage and civil partnerships since 29 April 2017; stepchild and joint adoption since 2017; constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination; UK responsible for defence; attitudes largely positive (90% consultation support).
